utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers representing the Prosecution today. With me is co-counsel Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink will join us in a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben is claustrophobic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think he's also proofing one of the witnesses for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones we are representing Mr. Naser Oric, and we have our legal assistant. Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you and your team too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries? No. A couple of -- there is this motion that was referred to yesterday by Ms. Sellers and that has arrived. That's a Prosecution motion for the testimony of witnesses via video-conference link planned for the 24th and the 25th of November. Have you had time to consider it by any chance, or do you require more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've received a copy this morning. We have reviewed it, and we will be filing a response opposing the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please try to file it as early as possible so that we decide on it before I go to where I need to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. We'll try to file it by the end of this week or before then in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The other matter is to our surprise we read through the correspondence that has been exchanged between you on the examination of Mr. -- that person anyway. I prefer not to mention his name for the time being. And about the appointment of a medical doctor. We don't like the way this has, you know, developed into -- into a causus belli when the whole exercise arose out of a recommendation that we made to try and agree amongst yourselves to seek the most economic and -- the most economic way of dealing with this problem rather than have the Tribunal involve itself in -- in money, appointing experts and the whole formality. You agree on a doctor. You obviously hasn't come to an agreement. In addition, it has also become a causus belli and a temperature gauge to an extent of pleasures or unpleasures, this pleasure is yet to come. So I think that if we do not have a definitive answer from you by latest tomorrow morning, then we will ask the Registrar to appoint a doctor himself. So -- yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would like to state in court that we received the latest Defence letter yesterday. The Defence provided a copy for us, or we received the copy that came through the mail, and we both acknowledged that it was a copy that had been unnecessarily delayed within the internal post, and the Defence and I have reached an agreement where we will now try and fax. So putting apart the issue of the correspondence having taken almost a week to get to us, the Prosecution was in a position yesterday to read that last letter. We are formulating an answer right now, and in the interests of practical efficiency and that we would like to move this issue forward, we would like our witnesses to be examined so that they can submit 92 bis (C) statements. We will be formulating a letter - we've already drafted it, it has to be finalised - accepting the Defence offer for their doctor. We would only point out that we regret some of the language that has been used in the prior correspondence in terms of political or ethnic background. Our interest is can we please have the witness examined and might we please reach a final resolution on our 92 bis (C) motion which has now been outstanding for almost a month. But just to inform Your Honours of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So basically do we take it that we can proceed with appointing -- not appointing ourselves, that you together could write a joint letter to this letter or the Victims and Witnesses Unit could inform this person? I don't know who is going to appoint him. We would be happy to receive a certificate from him, whoever commissions him. So the idea was to have both of you do that without involving the Tribunal in any -- in any expense. So if there is a way of doing it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think a joint letter could certainly be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, if that is okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think the Prosecution anyway would see any harm in having not only a joint letter and possibly an agreement on a joint procedure. And to our point of view it would be very important that we could set a deadline so this report could be before Your Honours and we could resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- in the joint letter you can actually say -- let's do it in a different manner, because this person will need to be paid and although -- and if payment is to be made partly or in full by the Tribunal in any case or by the Office of the Prosecutor, I think you need to have something in hand which would -- which would testify that -- that the Tribunal can proceed with paying this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. We would try and do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I would suggest is -- is Ms. Rydberg here? No. We could get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically I think what remains to be done is to establish -- in Brdjanin this used to be quite -- quite common and also easy to arrive at. To agree amongst yourself as to a protocol to follow on this issue, right? Whether it should be a joint letter, whether it should be one of you who would communicate, but on the understanding that the communication would be that this is something joint, that he is a person that has been -- he or she, I mean, is -- Senadine [phoen]. That he is a person that has been agreed upon by both -- by both parties and that for this you would need also to agree with him what his fees will be and then reach a protocol amongst you as to who is going to pay the cost. And then we can endorse it in a formal document without nominating him ourselves, because nominating him ourselves entails a special process. He would be an expert, and that would involve the Tribunal in a special procedure that needs to be followed. Like this will be all -- not evaded, but it would be a practical alternative which would put in place the exercise earlier and at much lesser cost. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour will propose that the Prosecution meet with the Defence after court today to try and move this forward as rapidly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we would be happy to accommodate whichever protocol you decide -- you decide upon. But it's -- it's something that you ought to agree upon. I mean, without any major problems. So we can bring in the witness. I understand that the witness has got a problem. I would just -- let's go into private session for a while. You can bring in the witness in the meantime. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: .2 (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This morning you will be giving evidence in this case in the proceedings the Tribunal has instituted against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before giving evidence you enter a solemn declaration in the sense that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a -- on a piece of paper that Madam Usher has just given to you. I would invite you now to stand up and read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. It is the equivalent of an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take your chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are now going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Richardson, who I suppose you have met already. She will then be followed by Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Naser Oric. I would like you to answer all questions as briefly as possible but also as fully as possible and certainly as truthfully as best, to the best of your knowledge. And when you say all questions, I mean questions which Ms. Richardson will put to you and questions which Mr. Jones will put to you. There is no distinction here between the Prosecution and the Defence. They have both got the right to ask you questions, and your responsibility under the law is to answer truthfully and fully. Did understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I will tell you what I know, and also it depends on how much I've forgotten. It's been 12 years since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, madam. Ms. Richardson, you can proceed, and you can lead the witness on the preliminary things so that we go faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, please confirm that you were born in 1948, you are a married Serb woman with four children, and that you and your husband are farmers for a living.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you live in the hamlet of Radijevici, and this is the village of Boljevici, municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to wait until the question is finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How long have you resided in Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I came to Radijevici when I got married in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is a -- a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many houses are in your hamlet of Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps about 25 or 26 houses, but there are a lot of people who have left, Serbs who had houses there, whose children had left. So there were some empty houses as well. That's about how many of us there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the surrounding village -- villages of Radijevici, could you tell us what the ethnic make-up is? Is this Serb or Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: The villages around Radijevici are mostly Serb villages, but there is also a Muslim village. It was called Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how far was Zanjevo -- is Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: From our village?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: About -- not much. There's another village there, Dijovici, which is even closer to Zanjevici. So it's Radijevici, Dijovici and then after that Zanjevo, but it's not very far away. I don't really know how to tell you in kilometres. It's not something that I ever bothered to find out, but it's all very close.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us in a matter of -- by minutes how far -- how long it would take you to go from your hamlet to the closest Serb village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: The closest Serb village to us on one side is Dijovici, and on the other side is Boljevici. It's all very close. Practically the houses run on. It's maybe about ten or 20 minutes away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to bring your attention to October 1992. Were you in your hamlet in that month, during that month?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And specifically did anything happen in that month?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What happened was that it was autumn. It was the 5th of October. We were there. Those of us who were in the village, we were gathering the corn in the fields. It was autumn. We were doing the farming work appropriate to that time of the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you with anyone?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: You mean in the field, when I was in the field. There was my husband and my mother-in-law, because of this attack, when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say "attack," could you tell us exactly what time did the attack take place?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: The date was the 5th of October, but I don't know what time it was. I didn't have a watch. We were working in the field, so perhaps it was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you tell us -- could you inform Your Honours how you were aware, what made you aware that your hamlet was under attack.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in the field, and we were gathering the crop, and then suddenly there was firing, shooting broke out, and I don't know. There was shooting. We ran out of the field, and then when we looked, we could see smoke from the neighbouring village of Boljevici. This is a little bit further away, but you could see it because it was a plane from the fields, the valley of the Drina. You could then see Popovici and these other villages. You could see smoke, and then burning and then we realised that there was an attack going on. There was nothing else we could think of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the direction that the attack came from?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. Our houses are just below the woods. The villages are all below the woods. The woods are at an elevation, and then from the woods we could hear shooting and shouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what villages are closest to those woods? Are they Muslim or Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: These were all Serb villages that were closer to the woods except for Zanjevo. Zanjevo is also close. But it was all really mixed. All the villages were -- actually, all the villages were Serb villages except for this one village of Zanjevo, which was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did -- did the shooting come from the direction of the Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in the fields, and as far as I could see, the woods were above our houses, so the shooting came from the woods. As you go along further towards Fakovici, that's where that village was, and then further along there are more Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you just testified that you heard shooting. Were you able to hear anything else or see anything else?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard firing. I could hear shouts. I could hear them shouting up from the woods, "Catch them alive."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you hear them say anything else?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, we -- we could hear them shouting, "Catch the Chetniks alive."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you see who they were? Were they civilian or soldiers, the attackers?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I was in the fields. We were in the fields down there, and my son came to help us pick the corn but then he went home to have lunch. And then when the firing broke out, I ran towards the house just to see whether he had heard what was going on and for him to come out so that we could flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not answering the question that was put to you. The question was: Could you see who they were? Were they civilians or soldiers, the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I started going, I didn't really reach the house. My son had heard what was going on, and I could see him running out. And near another house I saw several of them, and they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were they doing anything at this other house that you just mentioned, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: When I could see my son coming out of the house and I saw them, we started to run towards the Drina, but I could see that smoke was coming from that house, that it was set on fire, that it was burning, but I didn't see much else. We started to run, and we were running in the direction of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you got to the Drina, could you tell us what you -- did you encounter anyone at the Drina, other people?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I met some of our folks who were out in the fields, that's all. Some of them were running away next to the banks, and they were hiding. And I also met my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation with your brother?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked him where his children were. I didn't know that the children had crossed over to this side, because they were in Serbia. They had left. Some people had sheltered their children, sent them away across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: He said that the children stayed at home, and my mother. And he was going to see what was going on with the children, and he could see that the house was surrounded by soldiers. So he didn't dare approach and see what was happening with them, but instead started to run towards the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, while you were -- where does your mother live? Where is this house you just referred to? What village or which hamlet?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in Dijovici. Dijovici, over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While you were at the Drina River, were you able to see villagers from any other hamlet or any other village other than the ones you just mentioned, you just testified to?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our folks from the village, that's whom I saw. Those villages are very close by, and everyone tried to run towards the Drina River. You couldn't just walk at your own pace. You had to run fast to try to take cover, as fast as you could, because there was a lot of shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you see the other villages from the Drina, from where you were?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you -- when you arrived at the Drina, were you able to see what was going on in the other villages that are close to where you were?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see what was going on in the other villages because people had fled. They were running all over the place. You could see smoke rising from houses, houses burning. So that's as much as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell where these houses were, which villages these houses were in that you could see the smoke?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: We were out in the field, and I saw the smoke in Bonovici [phoen], in Popovici. Those were the villages nearby, the villages that we could see from our field. So that's what I saw, those specific houses and smoke rising from them. But as for the rest, I wasn't really paying attention. I was running and I wasn't paying attention to whose specific houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The villages you just testified about, are they Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Once people -- once you arrived at the Drina, what were you doing and what were the other people doing, once you got to the Drina?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Once we arrived at the Drina, we tried to cross the river into Serbia. Some tried to wade right through the river. Sometimes the tide was high, the water was high, but at that point it wasn't, so they held each other's hands, those who were a bit braver than the rest. So they tried to wade right through the river. And there was a boat taking people across. Boat loads. They were trying to take as many people as they could just so that people could be off.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you cross the river, and how did you cross the river?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I crossed on the boat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And once you arrived at the other side of the river, were you able to see anything going on, that was happening in your village or any of the other villages from the other bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: We were there just across the way from our village, across the Drina, and we saw houses burning. Not all of the houses had been set alight in our village. I specified in my statement that four houses had been set alight and the rest of the houses remained. So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, you testified that your husband and son was in the hamlet the day of the attack. Do you know if they were mobilised by the VRS, the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't. They weren't. We were there going about our business. My son was in Belgrade working, and he had come over for two days to give us a hand gathering the corn, and we were all there, civilians, out in the fields, and that's where it caught us. That's where we were when it started happening. And we were better off that way because at least we had time enough to run before the houses were fired on, because our houses were just next to the woods, and all the villages are linked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And on the day of the attack, was either your husband or your son wearing military clothing?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The other villagers that you were able to observe running, fleeing to the Drina River and the ones that you met at the Drina River, were they wearing military clothing?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. Not in our village or the surrounding villages where mostly elderly people lived. In our village, for example, there's no opportunity for -- for young people to -- to get work. All those who could left as soon as they could. They would cross to Serbia and find a job there. So there were mostly elderly people living in our area. I said in my statement yesterday that in our village there were a lot of houses with nobody in them. The children had gone, and the old people had already died. So the houses stand empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the people that remind in your village in the month of October of 1992, specifically the 5th of October, what were the ages of these people?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, my husband and I were born in the same year, and then there were people who were older than us who were born in 1927 and 1930 or perhaps 1940, that sort of age. Mostly, like I say, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During the attack, did you see any of the villagers or your husband or your son firing at the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No. We were there, and all we did was run to the river, because that was our only way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, prior to the attack in October, were any steps taken by members in your hamlet to protect the village in any way? And what I mean by protect, protect the village from attacks.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure. We were not really expecting an attack. There were no warning signs. Had we been expecting an attack, we wouldn't have just gone out to the fields to do some work. We would have tried to take shelter earlier. And this way we were just caught there, picking the corn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, did you return to your village following the attack, after the attack, following October 5, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We returned. As I said in my statement, we returned to get some clothes because of what had happened to us. And then we returned to go about our daily work, because those who couldn't -- well, I'm saying there were many people who had houses over in Serbia, but those who didn't, they had to go back. They had to sow for the new crops, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the condition of the houses once you returned to your village and observe any damage that the houses received in the attack, and could you tell us what you observed about the houses?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, there were houses that had burned down, and those that didn't were pockmarked to a large extent. The walls were drilled right through with bullets, and it was like that, the houses were like that. And those that had burned down, those were gone because they were wooden slabs and wooden beams. So those houses that had caught fire properly, they just burned down, and they were gone, the beams on the ground floor and the beams on the upper floor. It all just went up in smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you go to Bajina Basta shortly after the attack in October, on October 5, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That is, we did. My mother-in-law had been there up to that point, and then we went, and we would go there and we would go back to work. It was autumn. We had livestock over there. We were caught in the fields. That's where we kept our livestock, and much of our livestock had then been taken away, many cows and sheep, during the attack. And some stayed at night, and we could hear them cry and moan, and moan at night. It was 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. It was dark enough so you weren't able to see. There was a storm coming on, lots of rain, and you couldn't really see anything. You could hear the individual cows that still remained. They were making sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you travel to Bajina Basta for any reason in relation to your mother, shortly after the attack?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of October, I did go. They called us. They came to gather the bodies, and they said that people should be buried over there, those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was your mother one of those individuals that had been killed?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any other -- the bodies that you observed in Bajina Basta, were you able to recognise them? Did you know them, who these people were?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, those that had been gathered from Dijovici and Boljevici, I knew those people. And for example, I had seen some at the morgue. I knew those people. I knew them while they were still alive, those people who were locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the injuries on your mother's body?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that really relevant to these charges? It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Rephrase the question, then, please. And also I took your previous question to mean that you were trying to get from the witness at least the names of the persons she might have recognised in the morgue, which she did not give us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could just tell us the names of the individuals you recognised from the morgue that day that you visited to attend to your mother.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. All those that I recognised, I can give you their names, from Dijovici. My mother, Stojka Stjepanovic. Then there was Milovan Djokic, Sreten Djokic. His son, Svetozar Djokic. Radovan Djukic, Vidoje Djukic; also his son. From Boljevici, Milutin Ristic, Stanija Vasic, her husband, Vladan Vasic. Zarija Ristic from Kutjesi. Petra -- I can't remember her last name. I can't remember her last name. The first name was Petra, but I can't remember her last name. She was from Kutjesi, this woman. From Fakovici, some of my relatives were there, and her daughter Slavka Markovic and her husband Radomir Markovic. Another man named Djokic, but he was married to a woman from Fakovici and that's where he lived. He was an elementary schoolteacher. There was a man called Benes from Stamatovici; we knew this man. And another man called Rade Savic. I knew those persons, and, well, just like that. I knew them, and I saw them. And they were all together there. As well as Miroslav Ivanovic, another person from Dijovici. Those are the persons I recognised. They were in the same sort of department, the same place, and relatives came to collect their own bodies for burials. The relatives came to be there, and each came to -- to get their own people and to take them on to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. From Dijovici, madam, you mentioned some five persons. Some of them are Djokic, like Milovan Djokic and Sreten Djokic and Svetozar Djokic. The other two, Radovan and Vidoje, where they Djokic or Djukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djukic, Djukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the interpretation arrived as Djokic earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djokic and Djukic. Radovan and Vidoje Djukic, and the other people were called Djokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I had heard you say Djukic. That's the reason why I put the question was to correct the transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: These individuals that you just mentioned, the bodies, you testified that some of them were from Fakovici, Dijovici. Were there any other villages these people were from that you know?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, those that I mentioned before, Milutin Ristic, Zarija Ristic, Vladan Vasic and his wife Stanija Vasic. Those people were from Boljevici, those people. Well, you know, it's all nearby, the same area, so I knew those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the people that you just mentioned that died, did they die in an attack on their village that occurred on 5th of October, 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: They were killed during the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: -- in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this attack on their village, did it occur on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know how your mother died?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, how she died, as people say, dead men can't speak, but I noticed wounds on her body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What kind of wounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I do object to this line of questioning. It seems the Prosecution is keen in this case to elicit details which are probably gory or at least upsetting to -- probably to this witness. I don't see what possible relevance they can have to crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Might I add something in that regard? As Your Honours are no doubt aware, there is a great deal of public scrutiny for this trial as with all trials, and my concern is not that Your Honours will hear evidence which I am sure you can banish from your minds, but certainly, for example, last week we heard evidence which was gory and which was widely reported in the media, and I'm very concerned that there will be perception that this trial is about these sorts of crimes, and that it's unfair to this accused for his trial to appear to be concerned with these sorts of crimes when in fact it has nothing to do with such crimes. That's my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It is clear that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of the question in any case?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the relevance is as to the attack itself, we understand that these crimes relate to damage to property. However, we are eliciting the entire events surrounding the attack itself, and I think to just listen only to the portion that relates to the houses doesn't tell the complete picture, and I think it is relevant to the right of attack itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't the fact that a number of people result having been killed during this attack enough for you for the purposes of your -- of your indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. However, we've heard the Defence allege that a number of these people were part of military formations and defence units, et cetera, and I think it is relevant to the manner in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, certainly not the witness's mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we certainly hope so. I'm not trying to -- I just want to make sure that this is not a question later on that the Defence will come back to say that, you know, that these people were in fact part of any type of military formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why don't you restrict yourself to just one question, asking the witness whether there were signs of external violence on -- on the bodies of the persons she saw in the morgue and leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would exclude that due to natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I make one observation, Your Honour. We will certainly of course establish where necessary that people who died were in military formations because that's highly relevant to the military background. So if my learned friend is trying to project that line of questioning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not be stopped for sure, Mr. Jones, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would certainly -- I was simply trying to establish that in fact her mother did not die from wounds that could in any way be interpreted as being part of any type of military formation, and if in fact she died while her house was burning, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But even so, even if the witness were to describe to you a bullet wound here and a bullet wound there and a stab wound there and an incision there, how are we going to establish how those wounds were caused? I mean, it's -- it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. I can withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just stick to the question of whether these bodies presented a scenario of possibly having died all together within the same time frame due to natural causes or whether they met with a violent death because there were signs of external violence and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Please feel free to -- to rephrase it anyway you like. But I don't think we really need to go into details, you know what I mean? Just to establish that a certain number of persons were seen by the witness in the morgue, we know who they were, and whether they had visible signs of external violence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, from what you are able to observe when you visited the morgue, did the bodies that you observed, in addition to your mother, have signs of any violence, that they died violently?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I was able to see, I saw my mother, and I stated yesterday what I had seen and noticed. I did see the other bodies in the morgue, too, because those were people that I knew. Some had been killed. This Svetozar Djokic, one of his eyes had been gouged out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: As for my mother, she was --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: -- cut right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment. Without going into the details, could you tell us from your observation, possibly with a yes --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these individuals wearing civilian or military clothing that you could see when you went to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During the attack, were you able to recognise any of the soldiers who attacked your village on October 5th?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't recognise anyone, not at all. When I started out, as I said, I tried to call my child to tell him to leave the house. I saw Radoje Bozic, and then we just ran to the Drina River, and I didn't see anyone again. At least those that I saw, I didn't recognise. I can't tell you if I did or if I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you later learn who was responsible for the attack on your village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: How on earth should I know? How should I know who was responsible? There's no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Or who had led the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, did you talk to other villagers or other people in your hamlet, and did they tell you who they believed was responsible for the attack?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, how am I supposed to know. I was never involved in these things. I never imagined that it would come to that. You try to live cautiously. You try to take cover. As I said, we never expected this attack in the first place, that it would ever take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are playing games here a little bit. Could it have been fellow Serbs that attacked your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs being attacked by other Serbs. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have excluded the Serbs. Who else could it be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the attacks, when they started burning things down and killing people, the Muslims, when the attack occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How -- why do you say it was the Muslims? What -- what reasons do you have? What justification do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the reason, the justification is that people were killed. Whoever -- whoever was found was killed. And Serb houses were set alight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is it a conclusion that you draw because of any particular reason? Could it have been anyone else apart from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know who else it could have been. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any shouting and words that were uttered in the course of the attack by the attackers? Did you hear them shouting? Did you hear them say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Well, no. No. I heard them shout things like, "Get them. Get them," and that was all I heard. Well, you know what it's like. You try to run as fast as you can. You try to take cover. You run for your life. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a further question, Ms. Bozic. If things like you told us happened, houses are burning, houses are burnt down, people are killed, is it normal or would it be, rather, the case that the people would talk about the question who may have caused all these problems? Would everybody think it happened and just leave it, or would it, rather, be the case that people would try to find out who had committed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whoever attacked the village -- the Muslims attacked the people, that's what people said. And those were the people killed, and things were set alight. Not all the houses burned down. There were houses that remained standing, but there were also houses that were burned down in those villages. The attack -- well, at the same time there was an attack along the axis from Grabovacka Rijeka to Zlijebovac. It was all on the same axis, and all of those villages were attacked at the same time. It was all nearby. It was the Drina River valley, and it was all along the same axis. All those villages were lying along the same axis. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if you think the Muslims have done it, wouldn't it be normal that the villagers would think about which Muslims could have done it, from which other village or somehow try to identify those who have committed the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I didn't hear any stories, anything being said about that. People didn't really get together all that much. Everybody was very cautious after that attack. That's it. You do your work, you come home, it's like that. You do some work in the garden, in the house. We were there. But like I said earlier, the population was mostly elderly people. They were Serbs. They were working in different companies. And those of us who were there had to be there. We had to work. We didn't have anything else to make a living, no other way to make a living. We were just cultivating the land. There was no -- not much choice, really, for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one question to make sure. In Radijevici where you lived, the -- were there any Muslims living there in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, just for clarification, you stated that you heard the soldiers saying, "Catch them." I believe you also testified previously they also said the word "Chetnik"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And one final question. If you could tell us what the ethnic background of the people that you observed in the morgue was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead her. Were the people that you observed, whose bodies you observed, were they all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can start. I am not -- I'm asking you to start now because we have some appointments for our flu injections between -- during the break, so if we stop before, we will not be able to make those appointments. So go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm in your hands as to when you wish me to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stop at the normal time, 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, I'm going to be asking you some questions, so I hope you can see me all right. And you can hear what I'm saying, can you?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we'll just move the ELMO to make life easier. I'm going to -- thank you. I'm going to start by asking you some questions just about the area around Radijevici. It's right, isn't it, that your area is right by the Drina. I think you used the expression, "Uz Drinu."

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fields are close, our houses, our property, and then the Drina is right there. On the Drina itself, the village is below and then there is our property, the fields that we were cultivating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's good farmland, isn't it, that area?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's fertile land.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your village, it's not far from Fakovici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps, I'm not quite sure, but it's about three kilometres from Fakovici. But I'm not sure, but I did hear people say that it's about three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So not more than an hour or two's walk, perhaps, from your village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe an hour when you walk. You could get there in an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that Fakovici is a market village which you would have travelled to quite frequently?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: You mean like a cattle market?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Stock market.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where you would go with your produce and you would buy things?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: The market wasn't in Fakovici. There were about two shops there, but there was a livestock market where we took our cattle, you know. And that was usually on Wednesdays.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're familiar with Fakovici. You visited there many times, and you're familiar with the town. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Jones, but perhaps we are having some problems in trying to locate with a certain degree of precision where the witness's village was, and perhaps if she could be shown -- this is Radijevici and Fakovici. If she could be shown an appropriate map, and she would indicate to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it is definitely near the border with Serbia, near the border with Serbia. But if we can show her a map, she can indicate to us where the village is. Was it between Ratkovici and Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which village do you mean? Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ratkovici is up in the hills far away. It's up in the hills. It's not close to the Drina. I'm talking about Ratkovici. I don't know anybody from there, and I've never been to that village. It's in the hills. I don't know that village very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a map. The only problem is it has some symbols on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have -- could I have that -- that one is better, yeah. Was it near Boljevici, near Abdulici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which one? The village of Radijevici? Which village close to which village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which was the closest village to the village where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The closest village was Dijovici and Boljevici. These villages continued practically one after another. They're not very far apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we are talking of somewhere between Fakovici and Rogatica, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rogatica. I've heard of it, but I don't know where it is. I think that's quite far. I don't know that part at all. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway. In other words, one of the nearest village was Boljevici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Boljevici is almost on the Drina River, across --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're close. We have the houses. Below the houses is our property, and then beyond that is the bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And beyond that is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we've -- we know enough now. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones. Sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, before the war, whether there were Muslims living in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. Before the war, the closest village was Zanjevo. It was a hamlet, but it was also called Abdulici. It was Abdulici on the map, but it was actually called Zanjevo. It's a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Zanjevo, before the war, there were quite a number of Muslims living there, weren't there? Maybe around 300 Muslims living in Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: It was quite a large village. I don't know the numbers exactly, but I know that it was a large village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it was Muslim, an all-Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And like you, before the war, they had farms and livestock, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all worked. We worked, they worked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Cows, sheep, chickens, ducks, all that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know, all the things that farmers have to have, including cattle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And crops as well. They had fields full of crops and other --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop there for the time being. We will have a 30-minute break. That gives us time to finish what we have to finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic, before the break we were just discussing your Muslim neighbours in Zanjevo and the fact that they worked the land for a living as you did.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it -- it's right, isn't it, that before the war you helped them with their crops, especially during harvest time, and they helped you with yours?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were friends with your Muslim neighbours in Zanjevo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You would visit each other for coffee, go to each other's festivals, each other's weddings, funerals, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would also go to see their boys off to the army. They would also do the same for us. For example, when they were sending off their sons to go to the army, we would go, and they would also come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So these are people who were friends of yours over ten, 20, 30 years.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were their neighbours. And I am born in Dijovici, so our property is mixed. There would be our field and then one of their fields, one of our fields. It was all intermingled. This wasn't the case so much in Radijevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So and it's right, isn't it, that you would naturally be concerned for their welfare, and they were concerned for your welfare?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was no hatred amongst us, no, before the war. There isn't any now either. There are people who have come back to live there, just as we have come back to live on our property. This is our living.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But in May 1992, it's right, isn't it, you noticed that the Muslims in Zanjevo had left their homes?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you have any -- do you know the reason why the Muslims left their homes in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you try to find out, given that these were your friends for 20, 30 years, and you were concerned for their welfare? Were you interested in what might have happened to them?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you weren't curious that friends of yours who you've explained you spent years together going to each other's festivals, seeing each other, helping each other, they disappeared and you had absolutely no knowledge and no interest in what happened to these people? Would that really be right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I didn't. We were over here working. We were busy with our affairs. I wasn't really interested in what was going on, how all of this came about and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You weren't interested in what happened to your friends?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: There were -- they had their reasons. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let's explore those reasons. Why would people leave their homes that they've lived in all their lives, and their fields which is their only source of livelihood, why would they leave those homes all of a sudden?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they left. They left. Our people left as well. That's how it was. I don't know the why and how of it. It's something that I cannot explain or tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, could it be that they were forced to leave their homes and forced to leave at gunpoint by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who would do that. What they were forcing, why they left, I don't know. From what I was able to see, there were no threats coming from our people who were close by. That's all. I don't know how they left, why they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: It's right, isn't it, that you saw Muslims up in the woods above your hills at night?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do I know? At night, when night falls, those of us who were there, we worked during the day. At night you just go to bed and you go to sleep. I really didn't look around that much. And even if I did, what would one see in the forest, in the woods? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you saw groups of Muslims in the woods after May 1992 when they disappeared from Zanjevo? So my question is: Isn't it -- isn't it right that you saw that the Muslims from Zanjevo who had gone off into the woods and hills?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I saw. We would see them, but I can't say that there was any talk. I can't say that there was any hatred or that we did anything to one another. I really don't know anything about that. I can't really say anything about it, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You know this area, and you've said how there's rich farmland down by the Drina. In your opinion, knowing this area, is it better to live on your farms with your livestock and crops, or is it better to be in the woods and hills above your village? What is the better place to live?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was better to live on your own property and to cultivate the land, which is what we did. That's how we made our living.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Have you heard of the expression "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've never heard of the expression "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Isn't it right - and tell me if you're not aware of this - that in April, May, 1992, throughout Eastern Bosnia Muslims were being expelled from their homes by Serb forces, and could it be that that is what was also happening in Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what they noticed and why they left their homes. I don't know that. I don't know. I can't say. I didn't get involved in that. In the village you live, you work, you're busy with your own affairs. You're thinking how to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're interested in politics in local politics?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS at the time? The Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, one moment, because -- one moment. Mr. Jones, again I apologise for interrupting you, but the interpreters did not catch her -- the witness's reply. Madam, be patient with me. Mr. Jones asked you whether you were a member of the SDS at the time, that is the Serbian Democratic Party. What was your answer? Because the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't a member of the party. To tell you the truth, I'm not really educated. I only attended four years of school. I never was involved in politics, nor do I know anything about it. I didn't get involved in that at all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. You went back to Fakovici sometime in 1992, as I understood it. Did you see a single Muslim in Fakovici after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't really go out all that much. When you'd go to Fakovici, you wouldn't really see that much. I really didn't go around that much. You would stay around the houses or go to the fields and so on. There wasn't really that much moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just so you understand, Mrs. Bozic, if I'm pausing, it's because we're waiting for interpretation. I'm going to mention some names of -- of Muslims from Fakovici and tell me if you know any of them. Himzo Suljic.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean Suljic? How do you mean? From where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know Himzo Suljic, and while I'm at it, Neva Ridjic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: From which village? There were no Himzo Suljics in Fakovici. I only know about the Muslims who lived in Zanjevo. But in Fakovici, there were Serbs. Fakovici was inhabited by Serbs. I don't know about Suljics there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're saying before the war there were no Muslims living in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: There were no Muslims in Fakovici. They lived in Zanjevo. And there were Serb houses in Fakovici. There aren't too much houses in Fakovici anyway, but it was inhabited by Serbs. There was a school there. Our children went to school there. There's a post office. There's a church. It's like a little place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your evidence is that there were no Muslims at all living in Fakovici before May 1992, none.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Living there. No, there were no houses of theirs in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go back to the Muslims from Zanjevo briefly. You've -- it's your evidence that they left their homes in May 1992. You've told us they had livestock. It's right, isn't it, that when they left their homes they couldn't take all their livestock with them? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had cattle. When you live in the village, of course you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is when they left, when the Muslims from Zanjevo left their homes and farms, they didn't walk off with all their sheeps and goats and chickens and ducks, did they? They had to leave those behind.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do I know. To tell you the truth, we are close, but I wasn't really that interested if they took any cattle with them, if they sent it somewhere else. I really don't know. I didn't go to see what was left behind. I don't know about the cattle. I really didn't wander around that much to see if anything was left behind, what was left behind, how much cattle they had, if they took it with them, where they put the cattle. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it the fact that they couldn't take their cattle with them, and that Serbs, their neighbours, took, stole the cattle and livestock that they left behind? Isn't that what happened, and isn't that something which you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: It's like this: What I know is that in my village, nobody took this cattle or brought it to their own stable or barn. Out of the people that I know there, I know that none of our people did anything like that. None of my folks did anything like that. I cannot say that they went and they took the cattle. This is as far as my neighbours, those who were living close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Serbs in Fakovici or Popovici or Boljevici, they might have taken the cattle left behind by the Muslims from Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's merely speculative, let's drop it. Perhaps you can rephrase it and ask her whether she knows of anyone else apart from the ones she has restricted her answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether Serbs -- are you aware of Serbs in some of the other hamlets, Boljevici, Popovici, Kutjesi, Fakovici who did take the property of Muslims from Zanjevo when the Muslims had to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you're saying property. I would restrict it to cattle because that's -- or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Livestock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Livestock, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where I was, no one took anything. As for Fakovici and those places over there, I don't know. I didn't see anyone coming and going or anyone taking anything. I just didn't see that. But I do know that those from my village and from the surrounding area, no one brought anyone else's livestock along. And I didn't go further afield than that, so I didn't know. I never left my village unless you -- you had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's deal briefly with the fields of the people from Zanjevo. You said today that this attack on the 5th of October occurred during harvest time and that in previous years you would help harvest the fields of the Muslims and they would help you. It's right, isn't it, that this year you weren't helping your Muslim neighbours harvest their crops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This year. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be specific because she might misunderstand your meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In 1992, it's right, isn't it, that you didn't help your Muslim neighbours with their harvest as you did in previous years?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: In 1992. Well, you know, it -- they had sown the crops and it was there left standing and -- well, not that there were people around. Then we hardly had time to harvest our own crops, the corn, I'm saying. So some of ours was left standing, and then the next spring - that's after the next winter - we harvested the crops and theirs were left standing. It was there, it was ruined eventually. And then snow fell, and much of our crop was snowed over too. There were no people to harvest the crops, crops that had been sown. The next spring, people were back and they harvested their corn, the corn that we had sown and that was to be harvested in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that the Muslims from Zanjevo, that they neither could harvest their crops in October -- sorry, that they weren't harvesting their crops and that they couldn't get back to their crops because they would be killed if they went back there?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. Clearly counsel is asking the witness to speculate. I think she has repeatedly said that she doesn't know what happened in this village, and I think going through this line of questioning is asking her to speculate over matters she's not aware of,, and I think that the question either needs to be rephrased about what she's aware of, but certainly not going through again speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a suggestion I'm putting to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a suggestion to speculate basically, especially in the part dealing whether they would be killed if they went back there. You're pretending that she knows a little bit -- not a little bit, much more than she has actually shown that she knows. So go ahead, rephrase the question, but don't put the same question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm simply ask this then:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, that the field of the Muslims from Zanjevo were left unharvested that year, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll move on to another --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was left like that, like it was. Some of ours, too, because there was no one around after the attack. You weren't really free to move about that much or harvest the crops. There is the woods over there and above, and people were scared that someone would see them. Like I said, the people were afraid to do anything, but we have survived, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But you say that you weren't really free to move about that much. Can you expand on that a little? Why weren't you free to move about?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, not like before when we used to go to Fakovici and wherever. And then the way out was towards the Drina River. And whenever we needed something, we had boats moored over there, if we needed to go out and buy something, or to cross into Serbia where there were shops. We'd just go do our shopping and go straight back, and that's how it was. And that was our main way out, and that's where we usually went. We didn't move about too much because we were nearby. We didn't go to Skelani or to Bratunac. You had no means of transportation to use like there was before the war. Then we'd had buses and things, but now you couldn't. And you couldn't just walk there because it wasn't that nearby, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could keep your answers short that, would be helpful. Isn't one of the reasons at least why you couldn't move around --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One of the reasons why you couldn't move around is because there were lines against -- facing the neighbouring Muslim villages, firstly? That's right, isn't it, that there were lines established?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I know of no lines. We just didn't go, because you had no means of transportation. You couldn't go. Like I said, what was nearby was across the river. Whenever we needed something we'd cross the river, go into Serbia, and then go straight back. That was the extent of our movement because there was nothing you could use to go to Bratunac or Skelani in terms of transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you rising.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has apparently as best she could tried to answer the question, but certainly the question that was posed about lines, I think counsel needs to clarify exactly what it is he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's lines of defence, defence lines. Were you aware of any defence lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean trenches?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it more difficult. You see what you landed me in? Trenches is dug-up pieces of land that are dug up where soldiers stay, lay in waiting, to lay in guard their check and use as a cover.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. We didn't have that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you should move to something different, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to understand that in small villages in the area like it is in -- across the Adriatic, even in Italy and down south even in my country, people living in small villages, in hamlets, you will find that in their lifetime they haven't moved out of that village or that hamlet by more than sometimes five kilometres. In my -- in the village where I live in my country, there are small hamlets, and if you ask them which is the capital -- where is the capital city of Malta, they would tell you it's -- they think that the village which is nearby of which they form part is the capital. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour. At the same time, during war, information is at a premium, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you can rest assured that if you ask this witness how far she has been away from her village in her lifetime, it -- she will tell you that she has been very little, on very few occasions, and that's probably either a wedding or a baptism or something like that. And that's -- otherwise, they don't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why at the beginning I was asking how often she travelled to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Moving to a new subject. It's right, isn't it, that a village guard was organised in Radijevici and in the surrounding area at the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know, guards. No guards. Well, I'm just asking -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm telling you, there was no hate between us, and we weren't really afraid of one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall, Ms. Bozic, making a statement in 1994 before an investigating judge referring to these events?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I said yesterday they're telling me that there are two statements that they say I gave in Zvornik. I said I don't know. I only went to Zvornik once, and that was in 2000, I believe. But later I remembered that some people came. Which year did you refer to? 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I later remember that some people came to my home to see me. It was in the autumn, and again we were harvesting the crops, and they asked some questions. Well, truth to tell, I wasn't really involved. I did not know what would happen. I was not sufficiently interested to ask those people where they were from or what they wanted. They asked me some questions. They just told me, "Well, we're here to see because we heard that your mother had been killed, and we want you to tell us something about that, and please sign this paper." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're running on a bit. If you could keep your answers short and I'll keep asking, if you don't mind. Just to be absolutely clear, then, you're saying that you never gave a statement in Zvornik before someone who introduced themselves to you as a judge or with a court clerk present or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I did give a statement in Zvornik once. I told you I was there once, but they told me that I had been there twice for a statement, which is not true. I was only there once to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will you give me a moment, Your Honour, while I confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
