utterances.text: So as far as this statement in Zvornik is concerned, was is it, as far as you're aware, to a Judge, in particular Judge Vaso Eric, or was it to investigators or to police?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the man's name was, the one that I gave a statement to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a statement from 1994 in Zvornik which purports to be by you, and in that statement I'll read a sentence and see if you agree with what's said there. It says: "In the village -- in my village of Radijevici, as in the surrounding Serbian villages of Dijovici, Fakovici, et cetera, the locals organised self-protection. Guards were organised in the village and the surrounding area, and so my husband and sons took part in them." Now, first, do you remember making that statement; and secondly, is it true?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that I ever gave that particular statement. I said that my husband, we were in the village, but my sons were working in Belgrade, both of them since 1989 and 1990 respectively. As for that statement, I don't know. In 1994, in 2000, I didn't go to Zvornik then. I went later. But I can't know in which specific year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on from that topic. Now, as far as your immediate area is concerned, Radijevici, that at least is an area which you know very well, isn't it? You've walked around it your whole life?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during the war, it's right, isn't it, that you couldn't walk just wherever you liked because there were mines around your village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, we ploughed the land, the fields. You didn't do anything up in the hills. It was down in the fields, and we always worked the land. There were no mines in the fields. What do I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No mines in the fields. But were there mines, then, up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We didn't go to the hills. We didn't go to the hills because there was no need for us to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to place a document on the ELMO. It's ERN number 01317167. That's the Bosnian. There's an English translation, and it's from the Bratunac collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Technicians, please. I've asked the usher to put the document on the ELMO, the -- the original in the Serbian language for a change and zoom in so that will make it easier for the witness to read, because otherwise we'll have problems. Okay. I think for the time being that should be okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic, can you have a look at that document which has been placed next to you. It's in front of you, in fact, on the screen. Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want us to zoom in so that you get bigger letters, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you can see that, Mrs. Bozic, it appears from this document that a certain Radivoje Jakovljevic of the 314 Infantry Brigade of the VRS is from your -- first of all, was born in your village, Boljevici. So my first question is: Do you know that gentleman? Did you know him.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you aware he died in your village, Radijevici, during the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: He didn't die during the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. But it's right from this document, isn't it, and confirm whether you're aware of this or not, that in fact he died on the 15th of August, 1992, while reconnoitering the terrain in Radijevici village, and he was seriously wounded by stepping on a mine. Now, are you aware that that's how he was seriously injured?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he was killed. How he was killed, I don't know, whether it was a mine or something else that killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is someone who you've just told us you know, was born in the same village as you, who apparently stepped on a mine in your village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if she doesn't know, she doesn't know. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: She's aware that he died, and I'm putting it to her that surely she knows he was wounded in her village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that he died. He died --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection was to what Your Honour had just stated. I think the witness is clear that she doesn't know how he died and that counsel is insisting that she give him the answer that he seems to be seeking is unfair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's fair enough for me to press a witness as to whether that's the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if she's told you that she doesn't know, she doesn't know. I mean her, ask again if she knows how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How did he meet the Lord? How did he die? Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was on his way somewhere, but I don't know how. I mean, I was in the village at the time, and they started yelling he was killed. "He's been killed, Radivoje Jakoljevic." Now, where he was headed to or why, I have no idea. We were just going about our business. I don't know who he was with. I only know that he was killed. Whether he stepped on a mine or whatever. It certainly wasn't in the field. Maybe he was headed into the hills. Well, one thing's for certain, he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you aware that he was a soldier, Radivoje?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: How should I know? He was an elderly man. He was in the village, and he and his wife worked the land there. They had some property. They had some land. They had their own livestock. That's how it was. And he -- he didn't leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were VRS soldiers patrolling your area nearly two months before the attack on your village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't see anyone. I know that my husband didn't go anywhere. He never went anywhere, nor did anyone come looking for him. I didn't see anyone. There was no one. What I can say is that we weren't expecting that, what eventually happened. But that was the reason why no one was scared and no one was getting themselves organised. In our village, there was nothing much going on in terms of people organising themselves or an army being present. It was just villagers, farmers, who lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones, are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If that would be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's being admitted as Defence Exhibit number D41?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 42. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you one or two more questions on this subject. It's a pretty important thing, isn't it, if there are land-mines around your village for you to be aware of that, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not sure if there are land-mines or not. You just go about your own business. You walk around, you work the land. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to pursue it, Mr. Jones, but she's obviously not understood your question. The question was this: If someone like the army or -- or whoever put mines around your village in the hills where people supposedly could decide to go walking, wouldn't you expect to see signs saying, "This area is mined," or not? So that you are put on your guard so that you know that that area is mined and you shouldn't step inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we went wherever we needed to go. No signs anywhere that an area was mined. We went as far as we needed to go, and we did go wherever we needed to go, and that was the extent of it. Wherever we had to go in terms of our work and our property. That was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- move to a new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before the attack which you've described today, it's right, isn't it, that there was a lot of combat activity in your area?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you saying that you didn't hear shots or detonations from your village in the months before October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a peaceful area, isn't it, your village? There aren't the sounds of a lot of machinery or cars or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No, not really. It's not an area with factories or with any major industry. We live off our land. It's -- it's a poor rural area, no factories, no major industry. And everyone crosses the river to go into Serbia, all those who can leave, the children --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's a quiet, peaceful area, and you're saying that before October 1992, you didn't hear gunshots or detonations or any sounds of combat any period prior to that?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. Well, if we'd heard sounds of shooting, we would have been alerted and we would have tried to run away earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have another document which I'd be grateful if the usher would place on the ELMO. It's ERN number 01317139, again from the Bratunac Brigade collection. We actually have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic, if you could have a look at that document. This document appears to relate to a VRS soldier from the 314 Infantry Brigade called Zarko Bozic. My first question is: Given that it's the same name as yours, is this a relative of yours or of your husband? Zarko Bozic.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, what's your question about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was: Is he a relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Bozic, yes, a relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Zarko Bozic. Do you know him or did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it refers to him being active in the VRS since of beginning of war activities. We see at the top it appears that he joined the VRS in April 1992, and it says that he took part in combat in the area of Fakovici and Skelani. That's right, isn't it, that your village is between Fakovici and Skelani? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is: Were you aware the VRS - and in particular a relation of yours - being involved in combat in your very area since the beginnings of the war in April 1992, or is that something which you claim to be unaware of as well?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know. It wasn't in the village. Where was he supposed to be, Zarko Bozic. I don't know where he was. I don't know anything about that. I don't even know what went on in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, because this document does mention how, supposedly, he met his death, but there's no indication that it was in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It refers to him taking part in combat in the area of Fakovici and Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't say when.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. But one sees that he joined the army 18th of April, 1992 and that he died in January -- 9 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not in combat. It doesn't say he died in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed. But the inference is he was involved in combat in this area between April 1992 and January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're talking of eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's to establish that there was combat activity in the area at the time. It says: "Bozic Zarko has been in the RS army since the beginning of war activities. He took part in combats in the area of Fakovici and Skelani." And at the beginning of war activities one sees he joined the VRS in April 18, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. -- Madam Bozic, we have a piece of paper here which states that this relative of yours, Zarko Bozic, took part in combat activities in the area of Fakovici and Skelani any time between April 18, 1992, when he joined the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, and the day when he died, that is January the 9th of 1993. In these -- or in those eight months, do you remember any fighting, any combat -- combats or any fighting taking place or any attacks taking place in the area of Fakovici and Skelani? My question to you: Had the war arrived in Skelani and Fakovici between -- any time between April the 18th of 1992 and January the 9th of 1993, or had they been spared completely from the scourge of combat and war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fighting, combat, when he was there he drowned in the Drina, Zarko Bozic, this man, because they took a boat across the river to do some shopping over there, and the boat turned over and they all drowned. It keeled over. I was there, too. There were three or four of us women and three men. They were on their way to Serbia to do some shopping, and I was there too. I was on my way. I stopped by a woman in Banovic and the boat keeled over, and that's when he was killed. That was on the 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says the shopping was for the needs of his unit. So in fact it was shopping for a military unit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, not for any unit. What unit? They were on their way to go there or perhaps longer. His grandfather and grandmother and his father and mother, because his father was also unable, and he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for this exhibit to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I don't think the witness finished her answer about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, she hasn't. In fact I'm going to pursue it myself. This document will be D43, please. You haven't answered the question, madam. If you are getting tired, we stop, we give you a break, if you think you need a break. But the question was: Between April of 1992 and January of 1993, was there any fighting in the area of Fakovici and Skelani in those eight months, April 1992 to January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no fighting where we were. I began to tell you that he was on the Drina. He was going across. He had put some hay in the boat, you know, hay for the cattle, because he had a grandfather and grandmother across the other side who had cows. So they were taking the food across to Serbia. The level of the Drina was high. The boat turned over, and there were a lot of people there from our village. Well, not a lot, but there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You are going to be here a very long time if you don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not interested in how he was killed. I'm only interested in knowing whether between April 1992 and January 1993 there was any fighting that you know of in the area of Fakovici and Skelani. And just answer "yes" or "no" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993. Up until the 9th of January, 1993, there was no fighting. Where we were there was no fighting. Since the attack on the 5th of October, there was no more fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you can move to the next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you weren't a member of the SDS, is that right, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I wasn't. I don't even know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher to place the next document on the ELMO. It's ERN number 00835851. It was from the EDS, electronic disclosure system. And there's an English translation. If the witness could look at that document. Specifically if the witness could look at number 1015 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see 1015, Mrs. Bozic? Novka Bozic, daughter of Marko, born in 1948. That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: According to this, you joined the SDS on the 12th of September, 1990. Is that right? Did you join the SDS in September of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked me to do that or -- I don't know anything about it. I -- I didn't join, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're saying also that you didn't pay 120 dinars to the SDS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you pay 120 dinars to any political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't remember. I -- nobody asked me for anything, and I didn't pay anything. I don't know. As far as I know, I did not, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did the SDS have a women's section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know that I was not a member of it. I don't know what party it was, and I wasn't a member of it. Nobody asked me for anything, and I didn't pay anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is right. Mr. Jones, she is all yours again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I would ask this document to be given a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be -- is being admitted into evidence as a Defence document marked D44.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Bozic, were you aware of plans to put Fakovici in the area in a new municipality of Skelani and for that municipality to remain in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's move to the attack on the 5th of October, 1992. I think it's right, isn't it, that the first thing you heard was shooting but that you didn't know who was shooting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you don't know who started shooting.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I heard shooting. That's when the attack happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that there was powerful resistance from your village in Radijevici to the attack?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put a sentence again to you which appears in -- in the statement which we have and tell me whether you agree with the statement or not. It's there stated --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, I know exactly what -- but I'll let you say. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask counsel to indicate which statement he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the 1994 statement to -- made in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, but she doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I omitted to mention that. And it's page 2 if Your Honours are following, the third paragraph. "The men of the village quickly organised themselves" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait. Because we've still not explained to her exactly what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is going to read out to you apart from the statement that the -- we have here that supposedly you made in Zvornik in 1994 and which was mentioned to you earlier on. You said you remember going to Zvornik once but only once. Now, Mr. Jones is going to read a part from it, and then he will ask you a question. If you want to see this statement -- do you have the original or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, Your Honour, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we don't have it either. But Mr. Jones is going read a part from it and then you answer the question that he will put to you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's here stated: "The men in the village," that's Radijevici, "quickly organised themselves and put up powerful resistance to the attackers who were thwarted and who directed their attack to the neighbouring village of Tivovici [phoen]. The Muslims managed to set fire to the houses of Radoje Bozic, Milic Bozic" -- apologies. "Obren Vasic, and Radivoje Katanic." Now, it's right, isn't it, firstly taking the second part that you saw that the houses of Radoje Bozic, Milic Bozic, Obren Vasic, and Radivoje Katanic had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I saw that the houses were set on fire. I said that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see. So that bit is correct. Now, if we take the first sentence I read: "The men in the village quickly organised themselves and put up powerful resistance," isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, no. There weren't even enough men to put up a resistance. We were fleeing towards the Drina. As I said, my child was at home. He had gone to eat lunch. He was in the forest -- in the fields. We had been gathering the corn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your answer is that that statement is incorrect. Did you make that statement to a judge in Zvornik or not, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I only gave a statement in Zvornik once. I don't know where that comes from. I think that this was in 2000. Well, it didn't occur to me to write down the date, but I was in Zvornik only once. And when I came here, I was told that there are two statements from Zvornik. I only went to Zvornik once and gave one statement. I don't know where this other statement comes from. It's something that is worrying me, this about two statements when I know that I only gave one statement in Zvornik, and maybe this was in 2000 or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact there is a matter which -- which we perhaps should discuss in the absence of the witness, and I don't know if this is an appropriate time, but we have similar concerns to this witness. It's a matter which does have to be raised at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest -- yes. Let's -- usher, let's escort the witness out for a couple of minutes and we deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I would like to know where this statement of 25th of March, 2000 to the Office of the Prosecutor was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- I asked for the witness to be excused. I wonder if I could address the Court on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want you to be -- pardon? Let's answer this question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assist the Court with answering that question. Your Honour, it became apparent yesterday as I was proofing the witness that what is being referred to as the Zvornik statement, the statement given to an investigative Judge, was not, in fact -- she, Ms. Bozic, claims that she did not in fact go to Zvornik. The only time she went to Zvornik was to speak is our investigator. So whenever she refers to the Zvornik statement is what she in her mind refers as -- as referring to the 2000 statement given to our investigator. I'm aware that there is a 1994 statement and it says it was given to an investigative judge in Zvornik. She claimed she never went to Zvornik, as she's already testified to prior -- previously. So that's where the confusion is coming in. I think if counsel would -- would identify exactly which statement he's referring to by saying the statement that you gave to the investigator without referring to Zvornik, it might -- it might clarify to her exactly what statement he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's more than a practical matter referring to the statement. It's the fact that this is the second witness who has completely denied ever making a statement before in Zvornik in 1994. Our concern is to know what -- what in fact is going on here, because she is saying that she hasn't given a statement to a junk in Zvornik and yet we have a document which purports to be a record of a witness interview. And, you know, if this continues, if witness after witness is going to raise this issue, then something fishy is going on, and we feel it needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, usually these interviews by investigating judges in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we always had the -- we had the translations but we also had them in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we could locate an original. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because there would be a signature affixed and one could control better. I am very much suspecting at the moment that what has really happened, that what has really happened is that she did go once to Zvornik to make a statement, and that I think we can establish now more or less, I hope, with -- without great difficulties. And she did hint, however, that at a certain point in time someone went to her residence and she gave a statement there. Or she was interviewed there. That's how I understood her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not understand, however, that that was not referring to the witness -- to the statement given in Zvornik. I took it as -- as indicative of it being that statement. After all, the statement does not say that it was given in Zvornik. It only says that it was given to -- before an investigating judge of the lower court in Zvornik. So that in Zvornik is in relation to the office of that particular investigating judge. At least in English that's how I read it. It may not be like that in the original language, and I stand to be corrected. But I think we can bring in the witness and try to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think with this witness we may leave it there. It's matter which we'll continue to look into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. But indeed this is not the first case where this matter has arisen, and I don't know whether we are going to encounter statements made in the territory of the ex-Yugoslavia, statements made in Germany, statements made in several other places. So nothing to be excluded, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As -- as you just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can bring her in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's the witness who will testify as to what information she gave and who came to her home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's how I understood her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood her that at one time she went to Zvornik. Another time she was visited and she made a statement in her residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it will not be the first time that I have misunderstood a witness, and it won't be the last time either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want me to clarify it, I clarify it. Otherwise we move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. And we are going to continue now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, a few more questions. You've told us that you saw, I think it's your uncle's house on fire on the 5th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as you saw that, you were, as you said, fleeing for your life essentially towards the Drina. You were running to escape the shooting.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were excited, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Of course. I was afraid. I was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You weren't -- you weren't standing there watching events in your village. You were -- you were running away.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: We were running towards the Drina, and on that day we crossed over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think you said that the people you saw around your uncle's house were in uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I saw two or three of them in uniform, but this was very briefly because I wasn't close to the houses. I was in the field, and my son had gone to eat lunch. So I started running towards my house to call him so that we could escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's establish first of all how many people you saw around the house. How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Maybe three. Three or four. They were just below the house. Everything was happening very quickly. You know how it is. You're running to save your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So those three or four people, can you describe what each of them were wearing, whether they were wearing full uniform or a shirt or what precisely?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I really wasn't able to. I only saw the top part. I didn't see the bottom. Everything was happening quickly. I could see perhaps there were three houses away from my house and that house was burned, the house of Radoje Bozic. So that's when I saw them. And after that, we fled because everything was happening very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say three people and you only saw the top part. Were they all wearing camouflage tops or just one or two of them?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, they were wearing something with a pattern. I wasn't so close in order to really see what it was, but from what I could see, I could see that it was a multicoloured uniform. I openly saw them very briefly. After that we ran away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it olive-grey in colour or green or brown? What were the colour of the tops?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, it was green. Green. That's what -- how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could it be that one or more of those people were simply wearing green shirts or green tops as opposed to any sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I just saw something that looked like a top. I didn't see the shirts or anything. I wasn't close.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it possible that these could be three men wearing green tops but not necessarily wearing uniforms or being soldiers of any army? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was maybe afraid. I can't really say. Everything was happening very quickly. We were running towards the Drina, to the fields. You were just trying to get by.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then you mentioned three other houses which you saw burning, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I saw that one that was burning later when we were on the bank of the Drina River, because I said on a couple of occasions that the houses were below the woods. So I could see smoke coming from those other three houses, Milic Bozic, Obren Vasic, and Radivoje Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for those houses, it's right, isn't it, that you didn't see at all who might have started the fires if anyone did?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. All you could see was smoke from the roof. You could see it burning, but I didn't see. We were running, and then you could just see the smoke coming from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as the first house, your uncle's house is concern, it's right, isn't it, that you didn't actually see the people you mentioned setting fire to the house. You saw them among the house and then flames. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Around the house. I saw them around the house. I don't know whether those people set it on fire or someone else. I can't say. I didn't see it. But the house did burn down, and it -- there was a lot of smoke. It started smoking immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right also, isn't it, that there was a lot of gunfire that day. You've mentioned buildings being pockmarked with gunfire.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: There were not very big holes. You could just see it like that from the bullets. This was on those houses that did not burn down. We saw that once we came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it also right that as you were going towards the Drina that there was fire coming from Serbia, artillery fire, grenades, that sort of thing, being shot back towards where you were fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. There was nothing from Serbia that day when we were running towards the Drina. I didn't hear anything. That's where the village was. There was nothing of a military nature in Serbia. I didn't see or hear anything like that on that day. No, not that day when we were crossing over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've said - I think four times now - not at the time was there shooting from Serbia, not that day. When -- when was there shooting from the across the Drina that you were aware of from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear firing from Serbia, not where our village was, around our village. But I don't know if there was anything somewhere else. The Drina valley is large. There are many villages. I did not hear or see anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've said -- you mentioned these four houses suffering fire damage. That's out of 25 houses in your village, isn't it? In other words, the other 21 houses were not damaged? Sorry, could you answer the question audibly. The other houses, the other 21 houses in your village were not damaged on the 5th of October, were they?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, no. They didn't burn. Not all the houses burned down. In other villages, too, there were some houses that burned down and some that remained. In that village and other villages also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your house was all right, wasn't it? You went back there to get clothes the next day, so it was undamaged.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned today that some cows and sheep might have been taken. But it's right, isn't it, that you don't know who would have taken livestock from your village?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And other livestock remained which you said you heard moaning and crying. I presume that's because they weren't being milked. But no -- in other words, livestock remained in your village as well. It wasn't all taken.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, not all of it was taken. Some cattle was taken and some wasn't, because there was cattle out in the fields. They were grazing out in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have just one final question, one final matter. I wonder if the usher could please put the next document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I can take this matter in a few minutes and then I'll be finished with my questions, so perhaps it's appropriate to deal with this last matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I take that you are finishing your cross-examination now, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to know whether you have a long re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Pardon me. I don't have a necessarily long examination, but I think this would be a good time to take a break because I do have several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I suppose I will let Mr. Jones finish first and then we'll have a short break and try to finish unless there is a consensus from everyone that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to -- I've lost a couple of minutes now. I wonder if I could deal with this after the break because I will have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We will have a break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. You were about to show the witness a new document that you are seeking to tender in evidence, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the document, first of all, just with the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just ask you, Mrs. Bozic, to have a look at the first page of that document, the cover page, which is actually on the desk. The cover page. Yes. If I can ask you, Mrs. Bozic, just to look at that. That's the list of killed fighters of the VRS army of Republika Srpska. I want to ask you, today you mentioned people who died on the 5th of October, 1992, and so I'd ask you to turn to the first page of that document. Firstly, if you could just look at the top, the top row, and just correct me if I'm wrong, but you see there a number, last name, father's name, first name, year of birth, place of birth, date of death, place of death, and then a certificate number which we can come to later, and date of issuing the certificate, I presume that is. And now you'll see in this table that there are various people mentioned with the date of death of the 5th of October, 1992, and the place of death, Fakovici and Boljevici. And so what I want to ask you is you mentioned some names today. I'm going to take you to some names here, and you tell me whether that's the person who you were referring to. Firstly number 13 on the list, Milovan Djokic, born in 1935, Father Drago. Is that the person you referred to as having died on that day?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Milovan Djokic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Father's name Drago?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll go through the names fairly rapidly, so just correct me if any of the details seem incorrect. Sreten Djokic, number 14. And if he died on the 5th of October, you can just say yes.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Djoko Djokic, number 16. He died on that day? Yes.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Svetozar Djokic, number 18, you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that he was born in 1965?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to actually briefly deal with numbers 26 and 27, Ratko Djukic and Rajko Djukic. Is it right that they weren't -- that they didn't die on the 5th of October, 1992, but on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't die then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now number 31, Vidoje Djukic, son of Radovan. Did he die on the 5th of October to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now turn to page 6. I draw your attention to number 178. You see that -- push that up a little bit. Number 178. Oh, my apologies. It's difficult to see. Miroslav Ivanovic, son of Milan. Did he die on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that he was born in 1973 and so was 19 or 20 years old at the time?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Turn to numbers 303 and 304 on that list, which is page 9 in the English version at the bottom, and in Bosnian it's 3 303 and 304. And I think those are brothers, aren't they Radoje and Radomir Markovic, the sons of Stevo? Are they the Markovic brothers who you referred to as dying on the 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'd move to page 15 in the English, numbers 505 and 506, 511. Zarija Ristic, son of Novica, is someone you mentioned, isn't it, as dying on that day?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Milutin Ristic as well?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And number 511, Radovan Savic, son of Jovo?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that he too was a young man when he died? 27, suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 29, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. Math's not my strong suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that right? He was a young man when he died on that day?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally number 612 on the list, page 18 in the English, Vladan Vasic, born in your village, Boljevici. Again, someone who you say died on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it your evidence that these -- none of these people were soldiers when they died?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were civilians in the village. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Every single one of the names we've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you help us with what the -- the last column, the certificate and the date of issuing the certificate, do you know what certificates that might refer to? If you can help us with that, then fine. Don't worry if not.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You look at the document and you see the last column, certificate number, date of issuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's better. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before. I take it that you are tendering this in evidence, and this will be D44 or 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies for that oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I thank Judge Eser for drawing my attention. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic, you just testified that you know the individuals that counsel just -- the names of the individuals and as well as the individuals themselves who died in October of 1992. I would ask you to -- and that you are, excuse me, not aware that they were fighters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: They were there in the village. They were working there in their own village. They didn't go anywhere else. And then the attack, and then some were brewing brandy for the Slava holiday, and some were working the land. All of them were civilians. No one wore any military uniforms or equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to Milovan Djokic, he was born in 1935. Do you recall what he did for a living?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, he was working the land for a living. He lived off his land. He was a farmer. He did not have any other job. He worked the land. That's what he did. That's -- that was his livelihood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, couldn't you have asked this question before? How do you classify it as re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just seeking to clarify what Defence counsel -- what was raised by the Defence counsel as he went through the list, and certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He just asked a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether they were military conscripts or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only one additional question with respect to these individuals. Could I have one moment, Your Honour, just to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to make one remark with respect to the document that was just used to cross-examine this witness. We received this document -- we received the ERN number, I believe, of the document last night about 8.00 o'clock. We just received this morning -- just this minute the initial version. We'd not been given prior notice as I think should -- is what should be -- should be done in a case like this if you're going to use such an extensive document, and the Defence did not provide us with any notice last evening at 8.00 o'clock when they sent over ERN numbers, and today we're only now being provided with English versions of these documents, and so since counsel went into the list of individuals, made a point of -- a point of indicating their date of birth, I think it's -- I think it's only fair that this witness be allowed to tell Your Honours the approximate ages of these individuals as they were not all young individuals. Some of them were elderly, and clearly she's aware that they were people working in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we certainly will allow, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond as far as is this document is concern. We did, as has been the practice, send an e-mail to the Prosecution setting out the exhibits we intended to use, and we spoke to our learned friend this morning and we understood that no issue was going to be raised about possibly late service of documents. I'm surprised that having discussed that with my learned friend that it is now being made an issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only raise it now because counsel -- because you inquired whether -- why I had not used it earlier, and that's the only reason it's being raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I did not inquire why you had not used it earlier. I inquired why you did not ask the witness about details relating to each of the persons that she testified she saw dead in the mortuary on such-and-such a date in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am just seeking to clarify on re-examination her knowledge of these witnesses, who they were, and their date of birth, and what they did for a living, which I think it's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay. Go ahead. I don't think it's going to change much, but let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, you also testified that you know the individual called Zarija Ristic, and I think that's number 505 on the document that was shown to you. And is it a fact that you are aware that this person was born in 1928 and was elderly at the time in --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I know that he was an old man, but I don't know when he was born, what year. I know he was an old or elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did he do for a living?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: He was a construction worker, a bricklayer. He worked in the village on a farm. That was his occupation. He did not work in a company or anything. He was a bricklayer, a construction worker.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was he a member of the VRS, the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that he was. He was from Boljevici. We saw each other occasionally in the village. We both worked there. That's how it was. He was there in the village. Whether he was a member or not, I have no idea. I saw him wear civilian clothes. Our pieces of land were adjacent, and we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you recall seeing his body when you visited Banja Basta?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was he dressed in military clothing?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put this question already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put the question in relation to all the bodies that you saw in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to clear up with you, Mrs. Bozic, and for Your Honours as well, the two statements that you previously gave with respect to the events of October 5, 1992. Now, do you recall speaking with an investigator from the Tribunal in 2000 and giving him a statement?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If that's where the -- you gave him the statement, could you tell us? Was it in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik. I gave a statement once in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there -- did this individual that -- to whom you gave the statement, did he speak English and was an interpreter translating into your own language?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I talked. There was an interpreter who was interpreting for that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And prior to giving this statement, do you remember talking to anyone else and anyone else taking a statement from you regarding the events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I was being proofed yesterday, and that woman told me there were two statements that were made in Zvornik. I only know of one statement that I gave, as you said awhile ago. And then I remembered, but if I could imagine all the ramifications, I don't know. People came over. I went to the field to gather the corn. It was autumn, and I can't remember the specific date. One woman and one man came over, and they said, "Well, someone wants to see you back home." I was away from home for a while, but then I went back. And like I say, they told me that they needed some statements from me in relation to my mother's death. They came to see me at home. I didn't ask who they were or where they'd come from. They had an interpreter. And I just gave them my is story, something briefly, and that's what they wrote down and they left. I never asked them who they were and where they'd come from. I wasn't interested. I didn't want to know. I didn't check. Like I said, I didn't know. So those people left, and I went back to do work out in the field. And I only gave a statement once in Zvornik, like I said awhile ago. This person who had an interpreter, these other people, had not used the services of an interpreter. They just took a statement. They wrote something down and they were off. And that's what I remember. That's how it happened. Two statements, well, two statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. If I can just ask you to think back in your mind. Was the statement given to -- given to the two individuals who did not use an interpreter that came to your house, and this was in 1994, do you recall, or some -- sometime about that period?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the year was. I know they came. It wasn't long after the attacks. Whether it was 1994 I don't know. Please believe me. I simply failed to write down the date. I didn't realise that I would need it. Probably I would have written the date down, but I didn't because I had no idea what would come of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, when they took the statement -- you gave them a statement at your home. This is not in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. No, not in Zvornik, back home. They came to see me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify, they did not use an interpreter but they spoke in your own language?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did they tell you who they were and where they were from?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No. They told me nothing. Had they told me anything, I probably would now know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after you spoke with them, they wrote something down and gave you to sign and you signed it? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed. I did sign, but I didn't ask any questions, nor did I read the statement, nor did they read back to me what they had written down, nor did I request to read the statement. I paid no attention whatsoever to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, counsel previously asked you about portions of this statement, and I would only read this portion to you, and it's on page 2 of the statement that was taken on the 10th of October, 1994. The portion where -- that was read to you specifically stating that the men in the village quickly organised themselves and put up powerful resistance to the attacker who were thwarted and who directed their attack to the neighbouring village of Dijovici. Did you tell this to those two individuals who took the statement from you? Is that a correct statement? Did that in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And secondly, further down the page, on page 2 there is a single sentence towards the bottom of the paragraph, towards the bottom of the last paragraph, and I'm going to read this to you, and please tell us if this is a true statement: "The attack of the Muslims lasted 16 hours, and during that time I did not leave the house or see what was happening." Is this a true statement?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. That's not true. I didn't enter the house at all. I came there. I called out. I told you about how many statements I'd given. I called my child, and we -- he came out, and we ran straight to the Drina. It never occurred to me for a minute that I should enter the house. We just ran as fast as we could to find a place where we could take cover. I don't know. I didn't say that. I was never in the house for a minute. This really surprises me. I never entered the house to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the original?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have -- we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps if it is shown to the witness maybe she can tell us whether she recognises her signature, even though she has stated that she affixed her signature irrespective of the contents of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I do have a copy of the B/C/S. Unfortunately, I believe Defence was already given a copy of this as part of our disclosure and the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown her signature -- be shown the statement and also her signature portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask, Mrs. Bozic, if you recognise your signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise my own signature, and I did put my signature there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you didn't read this statement before you placed your signature? Just so that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And they didn't read it back to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Did they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- typewriter with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- they wrote it down by hand. I don't know. Well, I know they were writing something. Whatever it was, they were writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Writing or typing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That explains it. Okay. Of course, writing is one thing. Typewriting is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they had the machine with them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ms. Bozic, with respect to your membership in the SDS, as you were just asked previously by the Defence counsel, do you recall going to any political meetings in 1990 or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving a membership number from the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't have a number. I never received a number. I had no where to get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this the first day that you are learning that you were listed as a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: First I hear of it. I was really surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the men that you observed attacking your village that were wearing uniforms, when you first --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The evidence of the witness was that she saw men in green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Green.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if we start from that point, then my learned friend can develop from there, but we don't have evidence of men in uniforms at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But she never agreed with you that they were wearing the gear of some Irish team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour. But the possibility seemed open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe on direct the witness did state that these were soldiers and they were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The uniforms that you observed them wearing, were they similar uniforms? Did they look similar? In other words, the number -- you saw three to four of them, I believe. If I'm misstating your testimony, please correct me. And tell us if they were similar in likeness. Did they look alike?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it was only for a brief moment that I saw them. They were similar, but I didn't have time to just stand there and observe them. It was like I said several times, I only came a bit closer -- I came nearer the house for my child so that he could hear me and so that we could run away. I just saw them for a brief moment. Didn't make sense. And later on we withdrew towards the Drina. You couldn't see anything between the houses, who the people were, what they were wearing. I didn't recognise any one, as I said on a couple of occasions. I didn't identify a single person, first to be able to say who they were specifically. I just didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were previously asked about whether there was a lot of shooting going on in the village during the attack. Could you tell who was doing the actual shooting? Was it the people, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean shooting? When the attack took place, yes, of course there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, you saw people shooting; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go direct. Was it your own people shooting or the Muslims that were attacking the village, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was shooting from the woods above during the attack. That's when the shooting occurred. But I didn't see anyone. You couldn't just stand there and watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the shooting was in the direction -- in which direction? The direction of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the woods, that's where it came from. There is no village nearby for me to say that it came from another village. It was from the woods. And there are other villages further down, away from our village. I said yesterday there were those two Muslim villages. That was that. But that is in the woodlands, and it's far away from our village. There was shooting coming from the woods and that's what I knew, but it wasn't near the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were the people in your village shooting?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the house that you testified to earlier that you observed burning, the house of Radoje Bozic -- Bozic --

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- could you tell us what you saw when you first observed this house as you were fleeing? In other words, could you tell us about the soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw a couple of people there around the house, and then we just ran away. I know nothing about what was happening after that. I saw that the house had caught fire and there was smoke rising from the house. I didn't exactly go back to watch. We ran towards the Drina and we crossed the river into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was the house burning before the attack?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt from Denmark would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I understand that under the attack on your village four houses were burnt down, whereas the other houses, 20, 21 houses, were not burned but you could see where there had been bullets fired at them. Have you any idea why is it that only the four houses -- we have heard of other villages where all the houses were burnt. Have you any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Only four houses were burned in our village, but in the neighbouring villages some houses or many houses were burned, but not all were burned down. Some stayed, and some were burned down. So the same thing occurred in the other villages as in our own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did the men in your village have weapons, for instance, for hunting in the woods and so on? Was it common to have hunting rifles or guns?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, there were people who were hunting, and they did have weapons. A couple of people from the village had hunting rifles. I don't know if their rifles were there or whether they were in the houses, whether they were farther away. I don't know. But there were a couple of people from my village who were hunters before the war, and they're hunting now. Today they also go hunting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you -- when you say that there was no fighting in the way that there was no shooting from your -- from the Serb side, wasn't there any of those men who were defending their homes when you were attacked? In other words, did the men fly together with you towards Drina when you left or were the men standing behind in the village to defend the homes? Have you any idea?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: There were very few men in the village. I said that. Those who were there were mostly the elderly. There were some people from the villages that were getting ready for their family saint's day celebration. They stayed at home, but mostly those who were in the village were elderly people, except for those few younger people who were going to -- doing preparations for the family saint's day feast. They were going to shop and things for that holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did -- as you remember, did all the men, older and younger, did they flee together with you towards the river?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser from Germany would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bozic, would like to come back to the problem of the Houses. Part of them have been burned, others have not. Now, how do we have to understand you? Those houses who have not been burned down, does it mean that they have not even been set into flames or was it that the type of houses could not be burned down? So my question is: Have there been certain houses which have completely burnt down and other houses which not have been put in fire at all?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Those who were not burned down were not set on fire. The ones that were burned -- set on fire, they burned down. The other ones, the other houses, did not burn down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And you do not have an explanation why certain houses had been burned and others not?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I don't know anything about the how and why of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have another question. When you gave testimony with regard to Muslims who left the village, and you have been asked what happened to the harvest, to the crops and so on, you gave testimony that you did not have time to take care of these crops since you even didn't have time enough to take care of you were own crops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: With regard to the cattle, if the Muslims have left cattle, what happened to these cattle? I assume that cattle needs some sort of food. Did you leave the cattle on their own or did you give them some food or what happened? What else did happen to this cattle?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to that cattle there. I didn't go there to that village. I didn't go there from my own village. I don't know what happened with the cattle, who took it. All I know is that in my village, nobody brought any cattle into the village from there. I don't know if others did anything like that. I really cannot tell you anything, because I didn't go there. I don't know anything about it. To tell you the truth, I wasn't really interested. I was just minding my own business, working, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But isn't it rather unusual that people would perhaps let cry cattle for food and without doing anything about it?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if anybody went to do anything. But I didn't go, so I really cannot tell you anything about it because I don't know. I don't know. I'm really not aware of anything about that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. I have got a final question to you, madam, and then you can go. Do you know Naser Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I did know him before. This is a man from Zanjevo. I did know him. But -- I don't know. When the attack took place, I can't say if I saw this person or that person. There wasn't time to look and think. We were running, saving our lives. The people who were in the houses, they were killed. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know Edhem Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: That is also a person from Zanjevo. I knew him as well. It's elderly man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you know Ibrahim Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I also knew him. These were all people from Zanjevo. That wasn't so far from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did anyone mention these names to you as having been involved in the attack on the village where your mother lived?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: No. No. Nobody told me that they recognised them. Nobody told me that, and I -- well, there's a creek, and then on the other side of the creek there's a village. There's that village. So I can't really say that I recognised anyone or that anyone told me that those people were there. No, nobody told me anything like that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever mention these names to the two persons, that man and a woman who came with the typewriter and interviewed you in your house? Did you mention those three names to them?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that I mentioned them. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did they mention them to you?

utterances.speaker: NOVKA BOZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That brings us to the end of your testimony, Madam Bozic. On behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and of course on my own behalf, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher, and I can assure you that you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home. My last words to you is that on behalf of everyone present, I should like to wish you a safe journey back home, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So again once more I wish to thank you both for restricting yourself to the time schedule that we have fixed beforehand or we agreed to beforehand. Tomorrow we have another witness, and I take it that this witness will also last no longer than tomorrow. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right. Your Honour, may I just mention that we are very keen to have a witness list for after the break. It's vital for our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't give it to you myself. So I exhort the -- I'm sure that Ms. Sellers and her team will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll try and do that. As a matter of fact, we already have a temporary one, and of course it is dependent again upon certain things like videolink and witness line-up, but we'll certainly try and facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I think if you file the response on the videolink we can have it decided this week or early next week before I leave. That's -- we can decide also if we have this specialist neurologist visiting that witness. We can also decide on how to proceed, or whether we will have the 92(C) testimony or whether we could also possibly have a videolink with him. I mean, I don't know. That's another option that one could leave open. Yeah. Let's work on these matters, and I'm sure that the few days when we will not be sitting will be put to great use by both of you. I thank you. We will reconvene here tomorrow, same hall, same courtroom, okay, at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of October, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
